To properly treat the scorpion sting
To create a crisis so he can profit from the cure
To punish Kino for his earlier insolence

mcq.q: How does the town transform the moment Kino finds the pearl?
o: It becomes a predatory organism sensing opportunity.
It holds a celebration in Kino's honour.

mcq.q: Why does Juana insist the pearl is "like a sin" so early in the story?
o: She wants to keep the pearl for herself.
The priest told her so in confession.
She intuitively senses its destructive power.

mcq.q: How do the pearl buyers manipulate Kino's understanding of value?
o: They refuse to examine it at all.
They unanimously declare it worthless while colluding.
They send him to different buyers daily.

mcq.q: Why does Kino refuse to sell the pearl in the capital?
o: He wants to keep the pearl forever.
He refuses to be cheated by the local buyers.
He is too afraid to travel.
Juana convinces him to stay home.

mcq.q: How does Juan Tomas's warning about the "whole structure" function in the story?
o: It foreshadows the system crushing Kino.
It convinces Kino to sell locally.
It encourages Kino to fight harder.

mcq.q: Why does Kino beat Juana when she tries to throw away the pearl?
o: She stole it without his permission.
The pearl has corrupted his love into possessiveness.
He has always been violent toward her.
He values the pearl more than his family.

mcq.q: How does the destruction of Kino's canoe function symbolically?
o: It shows the attackers' cruelty only.
It forces him to become a farmer.
It cuts him off from his heritage and livelihood.
It represents his freedom to leave.

mcq.q: Why does the narrator describe the trackers in animalistic terms?
o: to show they are skilled hunters
to dehumanize them as tools of the oppressive system
to highlight their connection to nature
to make them seem less threatening

mcq.q: How does Steinbeck use the recurring motif of "songs" in Kino's consciousness?
o: as intuitive warnings of danger and harmony
as literal music played in the village

mcq.q: Why does the priest visit Kino only after he finds the pearl?
o: He needs Kino's help with repairs.
He genuinely cares about Kino's soul.
The pearl represents a chance for church donations.

mcq.q: How does the doctor's servant refusing "the old language" reveal colonial power?
o: It demonstrates internalized oppression and self-alienation.
It shows his education is superior.
It proves he dislikes Kino personally.

mcq.q: Why does Kino's vision inside the pearl turn from hopes to "evil faces"?
o: Juana convinces him it is evil.
His desire for wealth reveals its violent consequences.

mcq.q: How does the neighbour's envy function in the community?
o: It has no effect on anyone.
It isolates Kino and makes him a target.
It makes them pray for Kino's safety.

mcq.q: Why does Steinbeck describe the town as having a "nervous system"?
o: to show it is biologically alive
to prove it is sick and dying
to illustrate how news spreads and forms collective reaction

mcq.q: Why is Kino's dream of Coyotito reading "books as big as dogs" significant?
o: It reveals education as the ultimate symbol of liberation.
It shows Kino cannot read himself.
It shows his love for animals.

mcq.q: How does Juana's character foil Kino's throughout the novella?
o: She represents practical survival over dangerous ambition.
She is weaker and more fearful.

mcq.q: Why does Kino decide to lead the trackers away from Juana?
o: He reverts to a protective patriarchal role.
He wants to save the pearl alone.
He is tired of her company.

mcq.q: How does the death of Coyotito function as the story's climax?
o: It represents the ultimate cost of the pearl's corruption.
It makes the pearl more valuable.
It reunites Kino and Juana with the village.

mcq.q: Why does Kino throw the pearl back into the sea at the end?
o: The pearl has lost its beauty.
He rejects the entire corrupt system it represents.
Juana forces him to do so.

mcq.q: How does the beggars' "financial analysis" of Kino critique society?
o: It reveals how human worth is reduced to economic calculation.
It proves they are wiser than others.

mcq.q: Why does Juana walk beside Kino rather than behind him at the end?
o: He orders her to walk beside him.
The path is too narrow for two.
She is now his equal through shared tragedy.

mcq.q: How does the pearl's music becoming "sinister" reflect Kino's corruption?
o: His perception is warped by greed and paranoia.

mcq.q: Why does Steinbeck set the story as a parable rather than realism?
o: to give it universal, timeless moral weight

mcq.q: He worked deliberately, selecting the largest shells.
They wondered how such luck could come to any man.
He slipped his feet into his sandals.
It was a tiny movement that drew their eyes to the hanging box.
They knew his ignorance, his cruelty, his avarice.
He looked apprehensively to the east.
It is the bulwark against starvation.
A sad and contemptuous smile.
The beauty of the pearl cozened his brain.
He was not good at dissembling.
The town lay on a broad estuary.
A little furtive movement.
The doctor grew stern and judicious.
To see what the doctor would do about an indigent baby.
A lethargy had settled on him.
The pearl was ugly; it was grey, like a malignant growth.
Riding on the stalwart shoulders of his nephew.
A searing rage came to him.
Hundreds of years of subjugation were cut deep in him.
He was a man transfigured.
She made a flat damp poultice of seaweed.
He cried out in a guttural voice.
The shrill, keening cry of Apolonia.

sq.q: Who was John Steinbeck?
Who are Kino and Juana?
How did Kino find the pearl?
How did the pearl buyers cheat Kino?
How did Coyotito die?
How does Kino's "Song of the Family" show his true human nature, contrasting with the loneliness the pearl brings?
By refusing treatment without payment, how does the doctor demonstrate that even a basic human need like healthcare must be cashed?
How do the beggars' expert judgments on Kino reveal a social system that calculates human worth in terms of money?
Highlight the incidents that reflect the cultural hegemony of the colonizers.
How does every person in town, attaching his own dreams to the pearl, perfectly show as if it had some magical power?
Do you think, besides Kino feeling alone, the hunger for wealth cause a feeling of separation in the whole community?
How does ignoring Juana's free homemade remedy show the capitalist trick of believing something has value only if it has a price?
How does the "shell of hardness" that forms over Kino represent him being cut off from the person he used to be?
How does the servant's refusal to speak his native language show his internalization of the ruling class's culture?
How does the priest's visit expose religious activities being manipulated for economic gains?
How might Kino's aspirations for wealth be seen as false consciousness, adopting the values of the oppressors?
How does describing the town as a "colonial animal" reflect a view of society as an organic but conflicted whole?
How does Juana seeing the pearl as "like a sin" show her understanding of it as a physical object that brings destruction?
Do you think the town's collective surveillance of Kino demonstrates a repressive force enforcing conformity?
What is the metaphorical meaning of the pearl buyers secretly conspiring as a "market trap" to exploit the fisherman?
What does Juan Tomás's lament about being "cheated from birth to coffin" reveal about his class consciousness?
How do the neighbours' selfish speculations about the wealth reflect their false consciousness regarding class interests?
Do you think the priest's sermon about staying in one's "post" defends the exploitative, repressive colonisation?
What kind of loss of humanity happens when Kino turns into "an animal now" because of his chase for money?
What is the "whole structure" Juan Tomás fears Kino has defied, and why is this defiance so dangerous?
How does the burning of Kino's house represent the violent enforcement of class structure against challengers?
From what roles is Kino being alienated as he transforms from a family man to an isolated figure?
How does the pearl becoming a catalyst for violence exemplify capital's corrupting influence?
How does the family's fearful flight illustrate their alienation from their own community and its structures?
How does the "ancient thing", stirring in Kino, connect to a view of reclaiming one's real nature?
Does Juana's question about the dealers being right show false consciousness or a clear understanding of their situation?
How does Kino's proposed sacrifice reflect his internalization of the individual patriarchal characteristics?
How does Kino's "music of the pearl" turning "sinister" represent his working-class dreams have been poisoned?
How does the final confrontation between men function as a metaphoric reflection of larger class conflict?
Kino's seeing only "evil faces" in the pearl shows how its real worth has been destroyed by its price tag. Discuss.
Does throwing the pearl away constitute a true revolution against the system, or simply a retreat from it?
Is the tragic ending inevitable, or could Kino have kept the pearl to live a comfortable life?
